title: Payment System
problem: Design a payment system that charges customers via external PSPs (Stripe/Braintree), keeps an auditable ledger, supports refunds, and reconciles with the PSP daily.
summary: An idempotent payment API that sits in front of an external PSP (Stripe, Braintree) and a double-entry ledger. The dominant design choices are (1) client-supplied idempotency keys stored in Redis with SETNX so a retried charge never double-bills; (2) double-entry bookkeeping in a SQL ledger (DECIMAL, never float) so every debit has a credit and the books always balance; (3) orchestrator pattern that calls the PSP, records the ledger entry, and updates the wallet — with a compensating refund if any step fails. A nightly reconciliation job reads the PSP's settlement report and diffs it against our ledger so any drift is caught within 24h.

functional: Charge a customer's saved payment method through an external PSP (Stripe, Braintree, Adyen) and return a stable charge_id
Honor client-supplied Idempotency-Key: a retried POST with the same key must return the original response, never re-charge
Record every money movement as balanced double-entry ledger rows (debit + credit) in a SQL store
Process PSP webhooks (charge.succeeded, charge.refunded, charge.disputed) and update internal state exactly once
Support full and partial refunds that compensate the original ledger entries
Run a nightly reconciliation job that diffs the PSP settlement report against our ledger and flags drift
Expose a read API for charge status, refund status, and a merchant-facing statement
nonFunctional: Strong consistency on charge state — no user should ever see a ledger that doesn't balance
Idempotency window of at least 24 hours; same key + same payload returns the original response
p99 latency under 1.5s end-to-end, bounded by PSP (PSP p95 ~300ms is the long pole)
Durability: zero ledger row loss; 7-year retention for SOX and PCI audit
Availability 99.95% on the write path; the PSP itself is the next weakest link
PCI-DSS scope minimized: raw PAN never touches our servers, only tokenized payment methods

assumptions: PSP p95 latency: 300ms (external network + PSP processing)
7-year retention on ledger entries for SOX / PCI audit
estimates: Charge QPS: 1M / 86400 ≈ 12 QPS avg, ~35 QPS peak — tiny in QPS, huge in correctness cost
Ledger writes: 2 per charge (debit + credit) + 2 per refund ≈ 2.1M rows/day
Ledger storage: 2.1M * 365 * 7 * 200B ≈ 1.1 TB over 7 years — fits in one well-tuned Postgres cluster
Idempotency keys in Redis: 1M/day * 24h TTL ≈ 1M live keys * 200B ≈ 200 MB — trivial
Reconciliation batch: scan 1M rows nightly in <10 minutes

client.name: Client (Merchant checkout / mobile app)
client.summary: Merchant checkout page or mobile app that initiates a charge with a client-generated idempotency key.

sections.heading: Responsibilities
sections.body:
- Collect card details via PCI-compliant SDK (Stripe Elements, Braintree Drop-in) — never touch raw PAN
- Generate a UUIDv4 idempotency key per checkout attempt and reuse it on retry
- POST /v1/charges with Authorization, Idempotency-Key, amount, currency, payment_method_token

sections.heading: Idempotency key discipline
sections.body: The same key MUST be reused across retries of the SAME logical charge. Generating a fresh key on each retry defeats the entire deduplication system and is the #1 source of double-bills in practice.

sections.heading: Why this matters for beginners
sections.body: Money is not HTTP-idempotent by default. Network flakes happen — your response times out but the charge went through. Without an idempotency contract between client and server, retries silently double-bill.

bottlenecks.title: Idempotency key regenerated on retry
bottlenecks.trigger: Client code paths that generate a fresh UUIDv4 on each POST /v1/charges retry instead of persisting one key per checkout attempt; manifests on any network timeout (PSP p95 300ms, p99 800ms+ means timeouts are routine at 35 QPS peak)
bottlenecks.symptom: Customer double-billed — two captured charges with different charge_ids for one checkout; support tickets and chargebacks spike; reconciliation sees matching PSP rows but angry customers
bottlenecks.mitigation: Generate the UUIDv4 once at checkout form render, persist it in sessionStorage / a ViewModel field, and reuse across all retries until a 2xx is received; only rotate on user-initiated 'try again' after an explicit failure response
bottlenecks.detection: Server-side metric: count of distinct Idempotency-Keys per (merchant_id, payment_method_token, amount_minor) within a 60s window — alert if >1; also log client SDK version distribution to catch regressions

bottlenecks.title: Raw PAN accidentally touching client app code
bottlenecks.trigger: Developer bypasses Stripe Elements / Braintree Drop-in (e.g., custom form posting card number to own backend) to 'simplify' UX or debug; even one code path doing this pulls the merchant into PCI-DSS SAQ-D scope
bottlenecks.symptom: PCI audit failure, forced re-scoping of entire backend, potential fines; in worst case a breach exposes PANs that should never have left the browser-to-PSP tunnel
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce CSP headers that only allow card input iframes from js.stripe.com / assets.braintreegateway.com; code-review gate blocking any field named card_number/pan/cvv in request payloads; automated scanner on CI checking POST bodies to /v1/charges contain only payment_method_token
bottlenecks.detection: WAF rule at the LB that rejects (and alerts) any request to /v1/charges whose body matches a PAN regex (e.g., Luhn-valid 13–19 digit sequences); alert threshold: >0 per day

bottlenecks.title: Client-side timeout shorter than server+PSP p99
bottlenecks.trigger: Mobile app or checkout page sets HTTP timeout at 5–10s, but PSP p99 is 800ms+ and end-to-end (LB+API+orch+PSP+ledger) p99 can exceed 1.5s; under PSP degradation legitimate 15–25s responses are abandoned
bottlenecks.symptom: User sees 'payment failed' spinner and retries; server-side the original charge actually succeeded → either double-bill (if idempotency key rotated) or confusing 'duplicate' UX; elevated retry rate amplifies load
bottlenecks.mitigation: Set client timeout to 35s (longer than orchestrator's 30s PSP hard timeout) and show an indeterminate progress UI past 3s; on timeout, issue GET /v1/charges/:id with the known charge_id (or replay POST with same Idempotency-Key) rather than giving up
bottlenecks.detection: Client RUM metric for POST /v1/charges duration histogram vs. server-logged duration; alert when client-perceived-timeout rate >0.5% while server-side success rate is normal — indicates client giving up on healthy requests

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the client is called out as a component In most system designs, the "client" is a throwaway box on the left of the diagram. In a payment system, it's load-bearing. The reason is that **idempotency is a contract between the client and the server** — the server can't deduplicate retries on its own if the client doesn't cooperate by reusing the same `Idempotency-Key` across retries. The server has a Redis-backed idempotency store ready to catch duplicates, but it's keyed on something only the client can generate and persist. If the checkout page generates a fresh UUID every time the user clicks "Pay," the server sees each attempt as a brand-new charge and happily bills the card twice. ## What happens without disciplined client behavior Picture a customer on flaky hotel Wi-Fi. The POST to `/v1/charges` succeeds on the server, Stripe captures $49.99, but the response times out on the phone. The app retries. If it generated a *new* idempotency key, the server claims it in Redis (no collision), calls Stripe again, captures another $49.99 — and now the ledger has two captured charges, the customer sees two statement lines, and support gets a chargeback. Reconciliation *won't* catch this because the PSP and ledger agree; they just both agree on the wrong thing. ## The scale argument PSP p95 latency is 300ms and p99 is 800ms+. At 1M charges/day, even a 1% timeout rate means **10,000 retries every day** where the original charge probably succeeded. Without a shared idempotency key, that's 10,000 potential double-bills daily — a catastrophic failure mode the rest of the system literally cannot fix after the fact. ## The trade-off The designer accepted that correctness depends on client SDK discipline and PCI-compliant tokenization (Stripe Elements) — meaning merchants integrating badly can still cause incidents, which is why server-side metrics watch for duplicate-key patterns as a safety net.

lb.name: Load Balancer
lb.summary: L7 HTTPS load balancer with mTLS to the API tier.

sections.heading: Algorithm
sections.body: Least-connections across healthy API replicas. Payment POSTs are not sticky — any replica can serve any request because idempotency + ledger state is external.

sections.heading: TLS
sections.body: Terminates public TLS; re-originates mTLS inward. PCI-DSS requires encryption in transit for cardholder data, and card tokens count.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body: HA pair across AZs. A misbehaving API replica is ejected after 3 consecutive 5xx within 10s. Clients see at most one extra retry — which their idempotency key protects against.

gained: Rich retry / timeout / circuit-breaker policy per route

bottlenecks.title: TLS termination CPU saturation during retry storms
bottlenecks.trigger: Steady state is trivial (~35 QPS peak, well under the 50k concurrency budget), but a PSP degradation event (p99 >800ms climbing to multi-second) causes clients to abandon and retry; combined with mobile apps opening fresh TLS sessions each retry, handshakes can spike 10–50x to ~1500 handshakes/sec on a 2-node HA pair
bottlenecks.symptom: LB CPU pegged on TLS handshakes, new connections queue or get RST, healthy API replicas sit idle while clients see connection timeouts — looks like an API outage but the bottleneck is the edge
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enable TLS session resumption (session tickets with 24h rotation) and HTTP/2 connection reuse on the public listener; size the HA pair for 3x observed peak handshake rate; offload to dedicated TLS terminator (e.g., AWS NLB→ALB or Envoy with BoringSSL) if CPU >60% sustained
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on LB CPU >70% for 2min AND new_tls_handshakes_per_sec >500; also track tls_handshake_p99_latency_ms with alert threshold 50ms

bottlenecks.title: Aggressive health-check ejection during PSP slowdowns
bottlenecks.trigger: Current policy ejects an API replica after 3 consecutive 5xx within 10s; when the PSP degrades, orchestrator calls time out at 30s and API replicas return 504s in bursts — the LB can eject most/all replicas within seconds even though they are healthy
bottlenecks.symptom: LB reports 'no healthy upstream' and returns 503 to clients; on-call sees all 4 API replicas flapping in/out of the pool; charge success rate collapses to 0% even for requests that would have succeeded on cached idempotency replays
bottlenecks.mitigation: Distinguish upstream-dependency 5xx (504/502 from PSP timeouts) from replica-local 5xx; only eject on connection errors or 5xx with specific header X-Replica-Unhealthy; set outlier detection min_healthy_percent=50 so the pool never empties; add a separate /healthz that checks Redis+DB but NOT the PSP
bottlenecks.detection: Alert when healthy_upstream_count < 2 for >30s, and on ejection_rate >1 per minute; dashboard correlating PSP p99 with API replica ejections

bottlenecks.title: Single-AZ failure during AZ outage with slow DNS failover
bottlenecks.trigger: HA pair is cross-AZ but client DNS TTL and connection pooling mean an AZ loss can still black-hole ~50% of in-flight charges for 30–120s; at 35 QPS peak this is only ~2000 requests, but each represents a real charge attempt
bottlenecks.symptom: Half of checkout attempts fail with connection timeout during an AZ incident; idempotency keys protect against double-bills on client retry but conversion rate drops sharply; post-incident shows exactly half of traffic was affected
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use anycast or a global LB (AWS Global Accelerator, GCLB) in front of the regional HA pair so client TCP connects to the nearest healthy AZ in <10s; set client DNS TTL to 30s; ensure LB health to DNS propagation is automated (Route53 health checks with 10s interval)
bottlenecks.detection: Synthetic probes from 3+ external regions hitting /v1/charges every 15s with alert on any single probe failure >2 consecutive; per-AZ success-rate panel with alert on >5% divergence between AZs

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a load balancer for a payment system The Payment API is deliberately **stateless** — idempotency keys live in Redis, ledger state lives in Postgres, and any API replica can serve any request. That design choice only pays off if something in front of the replicas can spread traffic across them and pull unhealthy ones out of rotation. The LB is also the place where public TLS terminates and **mTLS** re-originates inward, which matters here because PCI-DSS requires encryption in transit for anything touching cardholder data — and payment method tokens count. Without a dedicated LB, every API replica would need its own public cert, its own health-checking, and its own DDoS posture. ## What breaks without it Point DNS straight at a single API replica and the first kernel panic, deploy, or AZ blip takes down checkout entirely. The operator sees a flatline on the charge success graph; the user sees a spinner that never resolves. Worse, clients may retry with *new* idempotency keys once they give up, and now the idempotency store can't protect you either — so an outage turns into double-bills during recovery. ## The numbers Peak is only ~35 charges/sec, which sounds laughably small for an LB. But TLS handshakes during a retry storm can spike 10–50x — roughly **1,500 handshakes/sec on a 2-node HA pair** during a PSP degradation. The LB's job isn't throughput; it's absorbing handshake bursts and keeping the pool from emptying when replicas flap. ## The trade-off The designer added an extra network hop (~1–2ms) and a piece of infrastructure to operate, in exchange for horizontal scaling, zero-downtime deploys, and a single PCI-scoped TLS boundary.

api.name: Payment Service API
api.summary: Stateless REST API that validates requests, enforces idempotency, and delegates to the orchestrator.

sections.heading: Endpoints
sections.body:
```
POST /v1/charges (requires Idempotency-Key)
POST /v1/refunds (requires Idempotency-Key)
GET /v1/charges/:id
```

sections.heading: Request validation
sections.body:
- Amount must be a positive integer in minor units (cents) — reject floats at the edge
- Currency must be ISO 4217
- payment_method_token must belong to the authenticated merchant
- Idempotency-Key header required on every mutating call

sections.heading: Idempotency fast path
sections.body: Before dispatching to the orchestrator, the API does `SET NX EX 86400 idem:<merchant>:<key>` with a small stub payload. If the key already exists and has a stored response, return the cached response verbatim. If it exists but is still in-flight, return 409 with a Retry-After.

sections.heading: Horizontal scaling
sections.body: Stateless → scale on CPU. Peak 35 QPS is trivially served by 4 replicas; real deployments over-provision for correctness incidents and traffic spikes.

gained: Strongly typed schema (protobuf) — fewer wire-format bugs in money APIs
lost: Harder for external merchants to integrate than plain REST

bottlenecks.title: Redis idempotency store outage fails all charges closed
bottlenecks.trigger: The API does SET NX on every POST /v1/charges and POST /v1/refunds before dispatching. If Redis is unreachable (AZ failure, maxmemory eviction, failover), the fail-closed policy rejects 100% of mutating requests — at peak 35 QPS that's ~2000 charges/minute blocked
bottlenecks.symptom: All /v1/charges return 503; checkout conversion drops to zero across all merchants simultaneously; on-call sees Redis client errors spiking in API logs while PSP and ledger are healthy
bottlenecks.mitigation: Run Redis in a replicated cluster (Redis Sentinel or ElastiCache Multi-AZ with automatic failover <30s); add a narrow fallback path that uses the charges table's UNIQUE (merchant_id, idempotency_key) constraint as the sole guard when Redis is down, serialized behind a circuit breaker so only a trickle of traffic uses the slow path; never silently fall through without the DB-level unique check
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on redis_client_error_rate > 0.1% for 30s, redis_p99_latency > 10ms, and api_5xx_rate correlated with Redis health; synthetic charge probe every 30s that exercises the full idempotency path

bottlenecks.title: In-flight idempotency key collisions returning 409 during PSP slowdowns
bottlenecks.trigger: When the PSP degrades (p99 climbs from 800ms toward the 30s orchestrator timeout), client timeouts fire and retries arrive while the original request is still holding the 'in_flight' marker. At 35 QPS peak with even 5% of requests stuck >10s, hundreds of retries hit 409 Retry-After per minute
bottlenecks.symptom: Spike in 409 responses from /v1/charges; clients that don't implement Retry-After back off poorly and hammer the API; support sees 'payment stuck' complaints even though the original charge will eventually succeed
bottlenecks.mitigation: Make the in-flight path a bounded wait (e.g., Redis BLPOP on a per-key notification channel for up to 5s) so a retry either gets the cached response when the original completes or a clean 409 with a computed Retry-After based on observed PSP p99; publish the completion signal from the API replica that wins the race
bottlenecks.detection: Track http_409_rate on /v1/charges with alert at >0.5% sustained; dashboard correlating 409 rate with PSP p99 latency; log the age of the in_flight marker at collision time and alert if p95 > 10s

bottlenecks.title: Request validation accepting floats or non-minor-unit amounts
bottlenecks.trigger: A merchant SDK serializes 49.99 as a JSON float instead of 4999 integer minor units; if the API's validator uses loose coercion (e.g., Python int(49.99) = 49, or JS Number handling), the charge proceeds with the wrong amount. Even 1 bug per 100k requests at 1M charges/day = 10 wrong-amount charges/day reaching the ledger
bottlenecks.symptom: Reconciliation flags amount_mismatch discrepancies 24h later; customers charged $0.49 instead of $49.99 (or vice versa); manual refund/recapture toil; potential regulatory exposure since the ledger recorded a different amount than authorized
bottlenecks.mitigation: Strict JSON schema validation at the edge rejecting any non-integer amount_minor (e.g., pydantic StrictInt, AJV with type:'integer' and multipleOf:1); reject requests where the raw JSON token for amount contains a decimal point by parsing with a custom decoder; add a sanity bound (amount_minor between 1 and 100000000) to catch unit-confusion bugs
bottlenecks.detection: Log and alert on any 400 from amount validation with the raw payload (scrubbed); metric schema_validation_rejections_by_field with alert on sudden spikes per merchant (indicates SDK regression); canary comparing amount_minor in request to amount in PSP response, paging on any mismatch

prebuild.explanation: ## Why there's a dedicated API tier here For a payment system that charges real cards via Stripe/Braintree, the API tier is the **enforcement point for the idempotency contract**. The client sends an `Idempotency-Key`; the API is the layer that claims that key in Redis with `SET NX` *before* anything touches the PSP or the ledger. It's also where you reject malformed money — amounts must be positive integers in minor units (cents), currency must be ISO 4217, and the payment method token must belong to the authenticated merchant. These checks have to happen somewhere stateless and horizontally scalable, because every mutating call needs them and they must run before the expensive downstream work. ## What happens without it Imagine the LB pointing straight at the orchestrator. Now a malformed request with `amount: 49.99` as a float reaches the PSP and the ledger — congratulations, you just charged $49 instead of $49.99 and reconciliation will flag it 24 hours later. Worse, without the API's Redis fast-path, a retried charge goes straight into a fresh PSP call. The user sees two charges on their statement; the operator sees an angry support ticket; the ledger and PSP both agree on the wrong answer so reconciliation can't save you. ## The number Peak is ~35 charges/sec. Each API hop is 3–15ms, so 4 replicas at concurrency 3000 is wildly over-provisioned — deliberately. The API is sized for **correctness under retry storms** (PSP p99 is 800ms+, so timeouts cascade), not for raw throughput. ## Trade-off One extra network hop (~10ms) in exchange for a single chokepoint where validation, auth, and idempotency are guaranteed to run.

idem.name: Idempotency Store (Redis)
idem.summary: Redis SETNX-backed cache of idempotency keys and their cached responses (24h TTL).

sections.heading: Key layout
sections.body:
```
idem:<merchant_id>:<client_key> → { status: in_flight | done, response_body: <json>, charge_id: ch_abc123 }
TTL: 24h
```

sections.heading: Atomic claim
sections.body: `SET NX EX 86400 idem:<merchant>:<key> {"status":"in_flight"}` — only one API replica wins the race for a given key; every other caller with the same key reads the cached result (or waits).

sections.heading: Response replay
sections.body: After the orchestrator completes, the API overwrites the idempotency key with the full response body. A retry within 24h gets byte-identical JSON back — no PSP call, no ledger write, no double-bill.

sections.heading: Failure modes
sections.body:
- Redis down → fail-closed on idempotency (reject the request, do NOT just fall through — that causes double charges).
- Key TTL expires before retry → treat retry as a new charge; the ledger uniqueness constraint (merchant_id, idempotency_key) is the belt to Redis's suspenders.

bottlenecks.title: Redis primary failover loses uncommitted idempotency claims
bottlenecks.trigger: Redis replication is asynchronous by default; a primary failover (AZ loss, OOM kill, planned maintenance) within the ~100–500ms replication lag window can lose SETNX claims that were acknowledged to the API. At 35 QPS peak with ~5% of requests in-flight during failover, ~50–200 in-flight idempotency keys can vanish — each one now re-claimable by a retry
bottlenecks.symptom: Customer double-bills appear 1–24h after a Redis failover event; PSP has two captured charges for the same logical checkout; ledger UNIQUE (merchant_id, idempotency_key) catches some but not all (if the retry arrives after the in-flight row was inserted with a different charge_id path); reconciliation sees matching PSP+ledger rows but duplicated from the customer's perspective
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use Redis with WAIT 1 500 after SETNX to force synchronous replication to at least one replica before acknowledging the claim, OR switch to DynamoDB conditional-put for idempotency (listed alternative: durable, no replication hole, +5-10ms latency acceptable at 35 QPS); always rely on the Postgres UNIQUE (merchant_id, idempotency_key) constraint as the authoritative guard — treat Redis as a fast-path cache only
bottlenecks.detection: Track redis_failover_events metric and correlate with a 24h-lagging query: SELECT COUNT(*) FROM charges GROUP BY merchant_id, idempotency_key HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 — alert on any non-zero result; also monitor redis_replication_lag_ms with alert >50ms

bottlenecks.title: In-flight marker orphaned by orchestrator crash blocks retries for 24h
bottlenecks.trigger: API writes {"status":"in_flight"} with 24h TTL before calling the orchestrator. If the API replica crashes (OOM, deploy, kernel panic) after the SETNX but before overwriting with the final response, the key sits as in_flight for 24h. At 35 QPS peak with even 0.01% crash rate mid-request, that's ~30 orphaned keys/day — each one blocks legitimate retries with 409 Retry-After
bottlenecks.symptom: User retries a failed checkout and gets persistent 409 Conflict for hours; support sees 'stuck payment' tickets where no PSP charge exists and no ledger row exists, but the idempotency key refuses to release; manual Redis DEL required to unblock the customer
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a short TTL (e.g., 60s) on the in_flight marker, extended by a heartbeat from the orchestrator while the saga runs; on final response, rewrite with the 24h TTL. Alternatively, store the API replica's instance_id in the marker and have a reaper job scan for in_flight keys whose owner replica is no longer alive (via service discovery) and delete them
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: redis_idem_inflight_age_seconds histogram — alert when p99 > 60s (orchestrator should never hold longer than 30s PSP timeout + margin); log count of 409 responses where the in_flight marker age exceeds 2 minutes

bottlenecks.title: maxmemory eviction silently drops idempotency keys before 24h TTL
bottlenecks.trigger: At 1M keys/day * ~1KB each (response body can be a few hundred bytes of JSON) = ~1GB live working set, well above the 200MB estimate if responses are included. If maxmemory is set with allkeys-lru or volatile-lru eviction instead of noeviction, memory pressure from co-tenant keys or response-body growth can evict idempotency keys before their 24h TTL, silently breaking the deduplication contract
bottlenecks.symptom: Sporadic double-bills where the customer retried ~hours after the original charge; reconciliation finds two PSP charges with different charge_ids for the same (merchant, amount, card) within a short window; Redis INFO shows evicted_keys > 0; no obvious error in logs since eviction is silent
bottlenecks.mitigation: Set maxmemory-policy to noeviction on the idempotency Redis instance so OOM fails requests loudly (caught by the fail-closed path) rather than silently dropping keys; size the instance for 3x peak working set (isolate from any other cache workload — dedicate the cluster to idempotency); store only response body + status in Redis, keep bulky metadata in Postgres
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on redis_evicted_keys_total > 0 (any eviction is a bug); alert on redis_used_memory / redis_maxmemory > 70%; periodic synthetic test that writes a key, waits 23h, and verifies it's still present

prebuild.explanation: ## Why there's a Redis idempotency store in a payment system Payments are the canonical case where "just retry on failure" is catastrophic. The client POSTs a charge, the PSP captures $49.99, but the response times out on the way back — so the client retries. Without a dedicated store tracking "I've already seen this request," the server has no way to know the retry isn't a brand-new charge, and the customer gets billed twice. The Redis idempotency store is the memory that lets the server say "I already processed key `7f2c9e4b-…`, here's the exact response I gave you last time" — no PSP call, no ledger write, no double-bill. ## What happens without it The failure is silent and expensive. A customer on flaky Wi-Fi retries checkout; Stripe captures twice; two ledger rows get written with different `charge_id`s; the customer sees two statement lines. Reconciliation *won't* catch this because the PSP and ledger agree with each other — they just both agree on the wrong answer. Support drowns in chargeback tickets, and the orchestrator and ledger have already done irreversible work by the time anyone notices. ## The number At 1M charges/day with PSP p99 latency of 800ms+, even a 1% client-timeout rate means ~10,000 retries/day where the original charge probably succeeded. The Redis store holds ~1M live keys × ~200B ≈ 200MB — trivial memory — but prevents up to 10,000 potential double-bills every single day. ## The trade-off Redis is fast but not durable by default, so the designer pairs it with a `UNIQUE (merchant_id, idempotency_key)` constraint on the ledger as a belt-and-suspenders guarantee.

orch.name: Payment Orchestrator
orch.summary: Coordinates the PSP call, ledger write, wallet update, and notification. Owns the saga / compensation logic.

sections.heading: Happy-path saga
sections.body:
```
1. INSERT charge row (status=pending) into ledger
2. Call PSP.charge(...) with our charge_id as idempotency key
3. On PSP success: UPDATE charge set status=captured; INSERT double-entry rows
4. Credit merchant wallet balance
5. Emit notification + Kafka event
```

sections.heading: Compensation (refund) on partial failure
sections.body: If step 4 fails after step 2 succeeded, the orchestrator issues an automatic PSP.refund to undo the capture. Every state transition is logged so reconciliation can prove correctness.

sections.heading: Why a dedicated orchestrator
sections.body: Putting this logic in the API replicas couples request handling to long PSP calls. The orchestrator can be throttled, retried, and scaled independently — and a crash mid-saga resumes from the charge row's state on restart.

sections.heading: Timeouts
sections.body: PSP call timeout: 30s hard, 10s soft with retry using the same PSP idempotency key. If the PSP is silent past 30s, we mark the charge `unknown` and let reconciliation resolve it — never guess.

gained: Durable execution — workflow state persisted per step

bottlenecks.title: Orchestrator crash between PSP charge and ledger capture leaves 'pending' charges
bottlenecks.trigger: Orchestrator process dies (OOM, deploy, kernel panic) after PSP.charge returns success but before the ledger UPDATE charges SET status='captured' commits. At 35 QPS peak with even 0.1% crash-window exposure, that's ~30 orphaned pending rows/day where money was captured at Stripe but our ledger shows pending
bottlenecks.symptom: Reconciliation (24h later) flags missing_from_settlement inverted: PSP has captured charges that our ledger records as pending; customer is billed but merchant balance is not credited; on-call must manually reconcile each row, decide whether to finalize or refund, and customers may see pending→silent-capture gaps on statements
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use a durable workflow engine (listed alternative: Temporal) so saga state is persisted per step and resumes automatically after crash; if staying with hand-rolled orchestrator, add a recovery sweeper that queries `SELECT * FROM charges WHERE status='pending' AND created_at < now - interval '2 minutes'` every 30s, calls PSP.retrieve(charge_id) with our charge_id as idempotency key, and finalizes or marks failed based on PSP truth
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: count of charges in 'pending' status older than 2 minutes — alert on >0 for 5min; dashboard for orchestrator_saga_duration_seconds p99 with alert >35s (longer than 30s PSP timeout means stuck saga)

bottlenecks.title: PSP timeout cascade exhausts orchestrator concurrency budget
bottlenecks.trigger: Orchestrator sim concurrency is 500. During PSP degradation (p99 climbs from 800ms toward the 30s hard timeout), each in-flight saga holds a concurrency slot for 10-30s instead of ~300ms. At 35 QPS peak, if average saga duration hits 15s, steady-state in-flight sagas = 35 * 15 = 525 — exceeds the budget and new sagas queue or are rejected
bottlenecks.symptom: Orchestrator queue depth climbs, API sees orchestrator-dispatch timeouts and returns 503s; legitimate charges fail even though PSP would eventually succeed; retries pile on making the problem worse; charge success rate collapses during what should be a recoverable PSP slowdown
bottlenecks.mitigation: Implement a circuit breaker per PSP (e.g., resilience4j or hystrix-style: open after 20 consecutive timeouts, half-open probe every 10s) that fast-fails requests once PSP is clearly degraded; shed load by returning 503 with Retry-After from the API BEFORE claiming an orchestrator slot; size concurrency for 3x worst-case saga duration (35 QPS * 35s = ~1250 slots) and autoscale orchestrator replicas on in-flight saga count
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: orchestrator_inflight_sagas gauge with alert at >70% of concurrency budget; psp_call_duration_p99 with alert >2s; orchestrator_saga_rejected_total alert on any non-zero rate

bottlenecks.title: Compensating refund failure leaves money captured without ledger entry
bottlenecks.trigger: Saga step 4 (wallet credit) or step 3 (ledger double-entry) fails after PSP captured the charge in step 2; orchestrator attempts compensating PSP.refund but the refund itself fails (PSP error, network, orchestrator crash during compensation). At 35 QPS with ~0.5% PSP failure rate, compensation is invoked ~150 times/day; even 1% compensation failure = ~1-2 stuck captures/day
bottlenecks.symptom: Customer is charged but merchant balance never credited AND no refund issued; reconciliation (24h later) flags as amount_mismatch or orphan_psp_charge; support tickets for 'I was charged but my order didn't go through'; ledger sum-check passes (no entries = balanced) but PSP settlement file shows captured funds
bottlenecks.mitigation: Persist compensation intent in a durable outbox table (`INSERT INTO compensation_queue (charge_id, action='refund', psp_charge_id, attempts=0)`) in the same transaction that detects the failure; a separate worker polls the outbox with exponential backoff and retries the PSP refund using the original charge_id as idempotency key until success or manual escalation after N attempts; never rely on in-memory retry for compensation
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: compensation_queue_depth with alert >0 for 5min and age_of_oldest_row >10min; count of charges where status='captured' but no ledger_entries rows exist — alert on >0 (invariant violation)

prebuild.explanation: ## Why there's a dedicated orchestrator in this payment system A charge isn't one action — it's a **sequence** of actions that all have to agree: insert a `pending` row in the ledger, call Stripe over the internet, flip the row to `captured`, write the double-entry debit/credit, credit the merchant's wallet, and emit a notification. Some of these steps are local and fast (SQL, a few ms); one of them is a 200–800ms external HTTP call to a PSP that fails ~0.5% of the time. The orchestrator exists to own that sequence as a **saga with durable state**, so that a crash or PSP timeout mid-way doesn't leave the system in a half-charged limbo. ## What happens without it Put this logic inside the API replicas directly and the first kernel panic or deploy that happens *after* Stripe captures the card but *before* the ledger UPDATE commits leaves you with money taken at the PSP and no record of it internally. The customer sees a charge on their statement; the merchant's wallet isn't credited; support opens a ticket; reconciliation flags the mismatch 24 hours later. Worse, without a single component owning compensation, a failed wallet update after a successful capture has no automatic path to issue the refund that would unwind it. ## The number PSP p99 is 800ms+, and at 35 peak charges/sec with saga durations sometimes stretching to 15s under PSP slowness, you can have `35 × 15 = 525` in-flight sagas simultaneously. That's 525 sequences each holding durable state across 5 steps — exactly the workload a dedicated, independently-scaled orchestrator is sized for. ## The trade-off An extra hop and a new component to operate, in exchange for the charge pipeline surviving partial failures without manual cleanup.

psp.name: PSP Gateway (Stripe / Braintree)
psp.summary: Abstraction over external payment service providers. Pool of outbound HTTPS connections to Stripe/Braintree.

sections.heading: Request shape (Stripe)
sections.body:
```
POST https://api.stripe.com/v1/charges
Authorization: Bearer sk_live_...
Idempotency-Key: ch_01HWX9ABC... amount=5000&currency=usd&source=tok_visa&description=...
```

sections.heading: Why pass our charge_id as PSP idempotency key
sections.body: Stripe and Braintree both honor an Idempotency-Key header for up to 24h. By passing our own charge_id, retries from our orchestrator hit the same PSP charge — we never pay for the same thing twice even if our process crashes between the HTTP send and the response.

sections.heading: Failure modes & latency
sections.body: External internet call — p50 200ms, p95 500ms, p99 800ms+. Baseline failure rate ~0.5% (network, PSP errors). The failure rate here is an order of magnitude higher than internal components and is the dominant source of unhappy-path complexity.

sections.heading: Multi-PSP strategy
sections.body: Route by geography (Stripe for US/EU, Adyen for APAC) or fall over on outage. Each PSP adapter normalizes responses to an internal `PSPResult` shape so the orchestrator is PSP-agnostic.

bottlenecks.title: PSP outage or regional degradation halts all charges
bottlenecks.trigger: Stripe or Braintree regional incident (historically 1–3 multi-hour outages/year) or degraded p99 climbing from 800ms to 5s+; at 35 QPS peak with 30s hard timeout, every in-flight charge holds an orchestrator slot and all new charges fail with no fallback path if only one PSP is wired up
bottlenecks.symptom: Charge success rate drops to near-zero globally; orchestrator concurrency (budget 500) saturates within ~15s; API returns 503s; merchant dashboards light up; support floods with 'payment not working' while ledger and Redis are perfectly healthy
bottlenecks.mitigation: Implement multi-PSP failover in the gateway abstraction — primary Stripe with Braintree/Adyen as hot standby; circuit breaker per PSP (open after 20 consecutive 5xx/timeouts in 60s, half-open probe every 30s); route new charges to the healthy PSP while open; normalize responses to internal PSPResult so orchestrator is PSP-agnostic; persist which PSP processed each charge for reconciliation
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on psp_error_rate > 2% over 1min per PSP, psp_call_duration_p99 > 2s sustained 2min, and circuit_breaker_state=open; synthetic probe hitting each PSP test endpoint every 30s with alert on 2 consecutive failures

bottlenecks.title: Outbound HTTPS connection pool exhaustion during latency spikes
bottlenecks.trigger: PSP p99 climbs from 800ms to multi-second under degradation; at 35 QPS peak, steady-state in-flight requests = 35 × avg_latency — if latency hits 15s, you need ~525 concurrent outbound connections, exceeding the gateway's default HTTPS pool (typically 100–200 per host) and TLS handshake CPU budget
bottlenecks.symptom: Orchestrator sees 'connection pool exhausted' or 'connection timeout acquiring' errors before even reaching Stripe; charges fail fast with internal errors despite PSP being partially available; retries amplify the pool pressure; success rate collapses well before the PSP itself is fully down
bottlenecks.mitigation: Size HTTP client pool for 3x worst-case concurrency (e.g., 1500 max connections to api.stripe.com) with HTTP/2 multiplexing enabled to reduce socket count; enable TLS session resumption to avoid handshake storms; use a dedicated connection pool per PSP host; set connection acquire timeout (e.g., 2s) distinct from request timeout so exhaustion surfaces as a clear signal; autoscale gateway replicas on in-flight outbound request count, not CPU
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: psp_http_pool_in_use / psp_http_pool_max gauge with alert >70%; psp_connection_acquire_wait_ms p99 with alert >100ms; tls_handshake_rate_per_sec spike detection

bottlenecks.title: Ambiguous PSP response (timeout after 30s) creates 'unknown' charges
bottlenecks.trigger: PSP call times out at the 30s hard limit with no response — at 0.5% baseline failure rate on 1M charges/day, that's ~5000 failures/day and a subset (~1% of failures = ~50/day) are true timeouts where the PSP may or may not have captured the card; the orchestrator marks these 'unknown' and defers to reconciliation 24h later
bottlenecks.symptom: Charges sit in 'unknown' status for up to 24h; customer may see a pending authorization on their statement with no corresponding order confirmation; reconciliation backlog grows; if orchestrator guesses wrong and retries with a different idempotency key, double-bill results
bottlenecks.mitigation: Always send our charge_id as the PSP Idempotency-Key (already designed) so retries are safe; on timeout, immediately call PSP.retrieve(charge_id) as a lookup probe with short 5s timeout — if found, finalize; if not found after 2 probes, mark unknown and enqueue to a fast-sweep reconciler running every 5min (not just nightly); never auto-refund or auto-retry with a new key on unknown status
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: psp_unknown_status_charges gauge with alert >0 for 10min; age_of_oldest_unknown_charge with alert >15min; daily count of unknowns resolved as 'PSP captured' vs 'PSP did not capture' to tune the probe strategy

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the PSP Gateway is here The problem statement says this payment system "charges customers via external PSPs" — meaning we are explicitly *not* running our own card-processing infrastructure. Actually moving money between a customer's Visa and a merchant's bank account requires being PCI Level 1 certified, holding acquirer relationships, and being on the card networks. Stripe and Braintree do all of that for us. The PSP Gateway is the thin adapter in our system that speaks their HTTPS APIs, normalizes their responses into a single `PSPResult` shape, and — most importantly — passes our `charge_id` as the PSP's `Idempotency-Key` so a network retry never double-charges the card. ## What happens without it If the orchestrator called Stripe directly with no gateway abstraction, two things break. First, switching to Braintree for APAC or failing over during a Stripe outage means rewriting the orchestrator. Second, if we forget to set the PSP idempotency header on even one retry path, a TCP reset between our process and Stripe turns into a double capture — the customer sees two $49.99 charges, support gets the ticket, and reconciliation 24 hours later confirms the PSP and our ledger both agree on the wrong answer. ## The number PSP p99 latency is 800ms and baseline failure rate is ~0.5% — roughly **10x higher** than any internal component (0.0005). At 1M charges/day that's ~5,000 PSP failures daily the gateway must classify (timeout vs. hard decline vs. network) so the orchestrator knows whether to retry, compensate, or defer to reconciliation. ## Trade-off We accept vendor dependency and per-transaction fees in exchange for skipping PCI Level 1 certification entirely.

ledger.name: Ledger DB (Double-Entry, SQL)
ledger.summary: Postgres/MySQL with double-entry bookkeeping. Every charge writes a matched debit/credit pair inside one transaction.

sections.heading: Schema
Double-entry invariant
sections.body: For every charge row, the sum of ledger_entries.amount_minor * (direction=='D'? +1: -1) across all entries must be zero. A daily integrity job runs `SELECT charge_id, SUM(...) FROM ledger_entries GROUP BY charge_id HAVING sum <> 0` and pages on any non-empty result.

sections.heading: Money type — never float
sections.body: `amount_minor` is BIGINT in the minor unit (cents for USD). Storing 19.95 as a float gives 19.949999… on some platforms and causes pennies-per-million drift. Use BIGINT cents or DECIMAL(20,4) — never double/float.

sections.heading: Why SQL, not NoSQL
sections.body: ACID transactions are the product here. The ledger transaction groups the pending→captured update with the two ledger_entries inserts; either all commit or none do. A NoSQL eventual-consistency store pushes correctness work into application code and reconciliation becomes much harder.

sections.heading: Scaling
sections.body: At 2.1M rows/day one primary handles writes easily. Shard by merchant_id when the hot merchant's row rate exceeds a shard's capacity. Read replicas serve reporting and reconciliation queries.

lost: Weaker constraint support than Postgres (no partial indexes, weaker CHECK)
Higher write latency due to Raft consensus

bottlenecks.title: Hot-merchant row contention on account_balances UPDATE
bottlenecks.trigger: The charge transaction updates account_balances for the merchant in the same transaction as the ledger_entries inserts. A top merchant receiving, say, 20% of volume at peak (7 QPS of 35 QPS) serializes on a single row lock; under refund bursts or batch captures the effective QPS on one row can spike to 50+/s with 5-30ms lock hold times, causing transaction queue-up
bottlenecks.symptom: Ledger COMMIT p99 climbs from ~30ms to 500ms+; orchestrator sagas exceed their concurrency budget (500) and back up; API returns 503s for charges targeting the hot merchant even though overall QPS is trivial; deadlock_count metric rises when refunds and charges interleave
bottlenecks.mitigation: Remove the balance UPDATE from the hot transaction — derive balance from ledger_entries sums with a periodic (e.g., every 1s) materialization job, OR shard the balance row into N sub-rows per (merchant_id, shard_id) with shard_id chosen randomly at write time and summed at read time; set lock_timeout=2s so contention surfaces as clean errors rather than indefinite waits
bottlenecks.detection: Postgres pg_stat_activity for long-running locks on account_balances; metric ledger_txn_commit_duration_p99 with alert >100ms; pg_locks query alerting on wait_event='transactionid' count >10; per-merchant txn duration histogram to identify hot accounts

bottlenecks.title: 7-year retention bloats primary, slowing writes and vacuum
bottlenecks.trigger: Retention target is 1.1 TB over 7 years in ledger_entries alone; at 2.1M rows/day the table grows ~770M rows/year. Without partitioning, B-tree indexes on (charge_id), (account_id, posted_at) balloon to tens of GB, autovacuum runs stretch into hours, and index maintenance on every INSERT adds latency to the hot write path
bottlenecks.symptom: INSERT latency on ledger_entries drifts from ~5ms to 20-30ms over months; autovacuum workers saturate and bloat accumulates; reconciliation scans (1M rows/night) that should complete in <10min stretch to 30+min; replica lag grows during vacuum-heavy windows
bottlenecks.mitigation: Declarative RANGE partitioning on posted_at (monthly partitions) so hot partition is small and old partitions can be detached/archived to S3/Glacier after 1 year while keeping queryable via foreign-data-wrapper or a cold-storage query path; set fillfactor=90 on hot partition; BRIN index on posted_at for reconciliation scans instead of B-tree
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on pg_relation_size('ledger_entries') growth rate and pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup > 10% of n_live_tup; track autovacuum_duration per table with alert >30min; reconciliation job duration histogram with alert p95 >15min

bottlenecks.title: UNIQUE (merchant_id, idempotency_key) index contention under retry storms
bottlenecks.trigger: This constraint is the belt-and-suspenders guard when Redis fails or a key TTL expires. During a Redis outage with fail-closed disabled, OR during a PSP degradation causing retry amplification, INSERTs hit the unique index hot spot and each conflict throws 23505 after a full index lookup — at 35 QPS peak with 10x retry amplification (350 effective QPS) the index becomes a serialization point
bottlenecks.symptom: Spike in 23505 unique_violation errors in Postgres logs; INSERT p99 on charges table climbs; orchestrator treats unique violations as idempotency hits but the handling path is slower than the Redis fast-path; effective charge throughput drops well below what the CPU/IO budget would allow
bottlenecks.mitigation: Use INSERT... ON CONFLICT (merchant_id, idempotency_key) DO NOTHING RETURNING id to avoid exception-handling overhead; ensure the unique index is the primary access path (or covering) so conflict detection is a single index probe; keep Redis fast-path healthy (see idem store mitigations) so this code path stays cold; consider hash-partitioning charges table by merchant_id to spread index hot spots
bottlenecks.detection: Metric: postgres_errors_by_sqlstate{code='23505'} rate with alert >1/s sustained 1min; charges_insert_duration_p99 with alert >50ms; correlation dashboard between Redis health and unique_violation rate to catch fast-path degradation early

prebuild.explanation: ## Why there's a double-entry SQL ledger here The problem statement literally asks for "an auditable ledger" that can "reconcile with the PSP daily." That means at any moment, for any charge that ever happened, we need to answer three questions with certainty: *did we capture it, how much, and does our record match Stripe's?* The PSP (Stripe) is not our source of truth — it's an external vendor that could have outages, replay bugs, or silent data fixes. Our ledger is the internal, legally-defensible record of every penny that moved. Double-entry (matched debit + credit per charge, summing to zero) is the invariant that makes reconciliation even possible: if the books don't balance, you know there's a bug *before* the PSP disagrees with you. ## What happens without it Imagine storing charges as a single row with a `balance` column. A refund bug double-decrements a merchant's balance; nobody notices for a week. When Stripe's nightly settlement shows $4.2M and our system shows $4.15M, you have no way to locate the $50K drift — every row looks plausible in isolation. The operator ends up running forensic SQL for days, customer support freezes payouts, and the merchant sues. With double-entry, the daily integrity check (`SUM per charge_id!= 0`) catches the bug the night it ships. ## The number At 1M charges/day × 2 ledger rows each + refunds = **~2.1M rows/day**, or 1.1 TB over 7 years. That fits comfortably in one well-tuned Postgres primary — no sharding needed until a single merchant's hot-row rate forces it. ## Trade-off The designer accepted SQL's single-writer ceiling in exchange for ACID transactions that group the status flip and both entries atomically — the one guarantee NoSQL can't cheaply give here.

wallet.name: Wallet / Balance Service
wallet.summary: Serves merchant balance views derived from the ledger. Keeps a cached aggregated balance per account.

sections.heading: Read model
sections.body: Derived from the ledger: `balance(account) = Σ credits − Σ debits`. For speed, a materialized `account_balances` table is updated in the same SQL transaction as the ledger_entries insert.

sections.heading: Why derived, not authoritative
sections.body: The ledger is source of truth. If the cached balance ever disagrees with the sum of ledger entries, the ledger wins and the balance is recomputed. This makes bugs recoverable without data loss.

sections.heading: API

bottlenecks.title: Hot-merchant row lock contention on account_balances UPDATE
bottlenecks.trigger: The wallet balance UPDATE runs inside the ledger transaction for every charge and refund. A top merchant receiving 20% of peak volume = ~7 QPS of the 35 QPS peak serializes on a single account_balances row; batch captures or refund bursts can spike effective per-row QPS to 50+/s with 5–30ms lock hold times
bottlenecks.symptom: Ledger transaction COMMIT p99 climbs from ~30ms to 500ms+; orchestrator saga concurrency (budget 500) backs up; charges targeting the hot merchant return 503 while overall QPS looks trivial; pg_stat_activity shows long waits on row locks for merchant_balance:<hot_id>
bottlenecks.mitigation: Shard balance into N sub-rows per (account_id, shard_id ∈ 0..15) chosen randomly at write and SUM'd at read; OR remove the UPDATE from the hot transaction and derive balance from ledger_entries via a 1s materialization job; set lock_timeout=2s so contention surfaces as clean errors rather than indefinite waits
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on wallet_balance_update_duration_p99 > 100ms; pg_locks query alerting on wait_event='transactionid' count > 10 on account_balances; per-account txn duration histogram to flag hot rows; deadlock_count metric on account_balances with alert > 0

bottlenecks.title: Cached balance drift from ledger source-of-truth
bottlenecks.trigger: account_balances is a materialized read model updated in the same transaction as ledger_entries. Any code path that writes ledger_entries but forgets the balance UPDATE (new refund type, partial capture, dispute adjustment), or a manual SQL fix that touches entries but not balance, silently drifts the cached value; across 2.1M ledger rows/day even a 0.01% bug rate = ~200 drifted accounts/day
bottlenecks.symptom: Merchant dashboard shows a balance that disagrees with SUM(ledger_entries) for their account; payouts compute against the wrong number; support tickets claiming 'my balance is wrong' that can't be resolved without recomputing from the ledger; drift may persist for days until noticed
bottlenecks.mitigation: Enforce balance update via a Postgres AFTER INSERT trigger on ledger_entries rather than relying on application code to remember; run a nightly integrity job SELECT account_id, SUM(CASE direction WHEN 'C' THEN amount_minor ELSE -amount_minor END) FROM ledger_entries GROUP BY account_id and compare to account_balances, paging on any diff; expose a /v1/accounts/:id/balance?verify=true path that recomputes from entries
bottlenecks.detection: Nightly integrity job metric balance_drift_count with alert > 0; sample-based live verifier that picks 100 random accounts/min, recomputes from ledger, and alerts on any mismatch > 0

bottlenecks.title: Read-path load on hot merchant balance lookups
bottlenecks.trigger: GET /v1/accounts/:id/balance served at ~1000 concurrency budget with 3–10ms service time; merchant dashboards and API integrations may poll aggressively (every few seconds per merchant) — a large merchant's dashboard with 50 admin users polling every 5s = 10 QPS on one account, and any read-your-writes requirement forces primary reads which compete with the hot-write row above
bottlenecks.symptom: Primary DB CPU climbs during business hours from dashboard polling rather than payment volume; balance GET p99 latency creeps up; in extreme cases read traffic interferes with the ledger write path on the hot merchant's row (buffer cache contention, autovacuum pressure)
bottlenecks.mitigation: Serve GET balance from a read replica by default; add a 500ms–1s per-account in-memory cache in the wallet service keyed on account_id (stale-while-revalidate); require explicit?consistent=true to hit primary for read-your-writes; rate-limit per-merchant GET to e.g. 10 QPS at the API layer
bottlenecks.detection: Metric wallet_balance_get_qps_per_account with alert on any account > 20 QPS sustained; replica lag monitor with alert > 1s; primary CPU% attributable to SELECT on account_balances via pg_stat_statements

prebuild.explanation: ## Why the Wallet Service is here The ledger already records every debit and credit, so in principle you could compute a merchant's balance on demand with `SELECT SUM(...) FROM ledger_entries WHERE account_id =?`. The problem is that a busy merchant accumulates millions of rows over 7 years of retention, and their dashboard polls for balance constantly. Recomputing from scratch every time is wasteful and slow. The Wallet Service exists to serve a **materialized view** of that sum — updated atomically inside the same transaction that writes the ledger entries — so "what's my available balance?" is a single-row lookup instead of an aggregate over millions of rows. ## What happens without it A merchant opens their dashboard and it spins for 8 seconds while Postgres scans years of ledger entries. Worse, 50 admins on one large merchant refresh simultaneously and the primary DB's CPU climbs from payment traffic into balance-query traffic — now legitimate *charges* slow down because read queries are competing for buffer cache with the ledger write path. The operator sees primary CPU saturation with no obvious cause; checkout latency rises across all merchants. ## The number At 2.1M ledger rows/day × 365 × 7 = ~5.4 billion rows over the retention window. Even with indexes, summing a hot merchant's slice of that is hundreds of milliseconds; the cached `account_balances` row returns in 3–10ms — **roughly 50x faster** — and the ledger remains the authoritative source if the cache ever drifts. ## Trade-off The designer accepted a second place to keep balance state (and the drift risk that comes with it) in exchange for fast reads, mitigated by a nightly integrity check that recomputes from the ledger.

recon.name: Reconciliation Job
recon.summary: Nightly batch that compares our ledger against the PSP's settlement report and raises discrepancies.

sections.heading: Input
sections.body:
- PSP settlement file (Stripe: daily CSV via Reports API; Braintree: nightly SFTP drop)
- Our ledger: all captured/refunded charges from the previous 24h

sections.heading: Algorithm
Why daily
sections.body: PSPs settle on T+1 and expose the settlement file after batch close. Running reconciliation nightly catches drift within 24h — fast enough to refund or re-capture before customer impact, slow enough to avoid thrashing on in-flight charges.

sections.heading: Output
sections.body: Writes a `recon_discrepancies` table; pages on-call for non-zero count. Typical steady-state: 0 rows. Anything above ~0.001% of volume is an incident.

lost: PSP webhooks are lossy; you still need a daily sweep

bottlenecks.title: Settlement report ingest exceeds 10-minute SLA as volume grows
bottlenecks.trigger: Design target is scanning 1M rows nightly in <10 minutes, but the job does a full Stripe Reports CSV download (~1M rows/day now) plus a ledger SELECT across a 24h window and builds two in-memory hash maps keyed by psp_charge_id; as volume grows toward 3M rows/day (peak 3x avg) or Stripe Reports file generation slows (p95 can be minutes for large accounts), single-process execution blows the window
bottlenecks.symptom: Recon job runs past 02:10 into business hours; on-call sees the nightly 'recon complete' signal delayed or missing; drift detection lag exceeds the 24h SLO so refund/re-capture windows close before mismatches surface; in worst case the next day's job starts before the previous finished
bottlenecks.mitigation: Stream the CSV via Stripe's file URL with chunked processing (never load 1M rows fully in memory); partition the diff by psp_charge_id hash across N parallel workers (e.g., 8) joining from a read replica via server-side cursor; set a hard 30min SLA alarm with automatic re-run on failure; pre-sort both sides on psp_charge_id and merge-join instead of building 2 hash maps (O(n log n) with bounded memory vs O(n) memory)
bottlenecks.detection: Metric recon_job_duration_seconds with alert >600s (the stated <10min target) and critical alert >1800s; recon_job_peak_memory_bytes alert >4GB; missing-heartbeat alert if recon_last_success_timestamp is >26h old

bottlenecks.title: Read replica lag causes false 'missing_from_settlement' discrepancies
bottlenecks.trigger: Recon reads charges from a read replica to avoid impacting the live write path; replica lag (observed 120ms in the flow, but can spike to seconds during autovacuum or heavy write bursts) means captures that committed just before the 24h window cutoff may not yet be visible on the replica when the job runs at 02:00, while the PSP settlement file already includes them
bottlenecks.symptom: Non-zero discrepancy count every night with kind='missing_from_settlement' or its inverse, all clustered near the window boundary (23:59:xx UTC); on-call pages on phantom drift that resolves itself when re-run an hour later; real bugs get lost in the noise and alert fatigue sets in
bottlenecks.mitigation: Wait for replica lag to be <1s before starting (poll pg_stat_replication.replay_lag); add a 15-minute safety margin to the window (scan 23:45..23:45 next day instead of 00:00..00:00) so boundary writes have propagated; OR run recon against the primary during the 02:00 low-traffic window (35 QPS peak is trivial, off-peak is ~5 QPS); tag every discrepancy with created_at-to-window-edge distance so boundary artifacts are visually distinct
bottlenecks.detection: Dashboard of discrepancy count bucketed by created_at proximity to window edge — alert only when non-edge discrepancies >0; metric recon_replica_lag_at_start_ms with alert >1000ms; correlate recon_discrepancies_by_kind with replica_lag timeseries

bottlenecks.title: PSP settlement file unavailable or schema-drifted at run time
bottlenecks.trigger: Job depends on Stripe Reports API (or Braintree SFTP drop) being available and on a stable CSV schema at 02:00 daily; Stripe has historically had report-generation delays of hours during incidents, and schema changes (new column ordering, renamed fields) ship without prior notice to API consumers; Braintree SFTP auth can silently expire
bottlenecks.symptom: Recon job crashes with KeyError/ParseError or hangs on report.file_url download; no discrepancies written for the day; on-call either gets a job-failure page OR worse, gets silence if error handling swallows the exception — meaning drift accumulates invisibly until caught by a later run or customer complaint
bottlenecks.mitigation: Treat PSP report fetch as a separate, retryable step with exponential backoff up to 4h and explicit failure alerting distinct from diff-logic failures; validate CSV header against an expected schema on every run and fail loudly on mismatch (don't silently skip columns); keep a fallback path using Stripe's /v1/balance_transactions API paginated (slower but schema-stable); persist the raw downloaded file to S3 before parsing so a re-run doesn't require re-fetching
bottlenecks.detection: Alert on recon_psp_fetch_duration_seconds >1800s OR recon_psp_fetch_failures_total >0; schema-hash check metric recon_csv_header_hash compared to expected constant, paging on mismatch; dead-man's-switch alert if recon_last_success_timestamp >26h regardless of failure mode

prebuild.explanation: ## Why there's a reconciliation job in this payment system The problem statement demands the system "reconciles with the PSP daily" — and there's a real reason. Stripe is an external vendor moving real money, and your ledger is a local Postgres table. These two sources of truth can drift: a charge can capture at Stripe but your orchestrator crashes before the ledger UPDATE commits; a dispute can close on Stripe's side that you never heard about; a webhook can be dropped. Without a job that periodically compares *both sides row-by-row*, you have no way to detect drift between what Stripe actually settled and what your ledger claims happened. ## What happens without it Imagine a bug in the orchestrator that occasionally writes a ledger entry of 4999 cents for a charge Stripe actually captured at 5001 cents. Every individual charge looks fine in isolation. A month later, Stripe's payout to the merchant is $50,000 lower than your system promised them — and now you're doing forensic SQL across 60 million ledger rows to find the drift, while the merchant threatens to sue. The ledger's double-entry check *won't* catch this because our internal books balance against themselves; only a diff against Stripe catches a mismatch with Stripe. ## The number At 1M charges/day × 365 × 7 years = ~2.5 billion charges retained. Catching drift within **24 hours** (not 24 months) means reviewing ~1M PSP rows per nightly run — small enough to finish in under 10 minutes, fast enough that refund/re-capture windows haven't closed yet. ## Trade-off The designer accepted up-to-24h detection lag instead of streaming reconciliation, because PSP settlement files only exist once per day anyway.

notif.name: Notification Service
notif.summary: Emits receipt emails, push notifications, and merchant webhooks after state changes.

sections.heading: Delivery model
sections.body: Orchestrator publishes a `ChargeCaptured` event to Kafka; a fanout worker fires the email, the push notification, and the merchant webhook. Each delivery is independently retried.

sections.heading: Why decoupled
sections.body: Notifications can be slow (SMTP, webhook targets). The orchestrator must never block on them — a broken merchant webhook cannot stall the charge pipeline.

bottlenecks.title: Slow/broken merchant webhooks exhaust worker concurrency
bottlenecks.trigger: Fanout workers deliver ChargeCaptured to merchant webhook endpoints whose p95 can exceed 5–30s or time out entirely; at 1M events/day (~35 QPS peak) even a few merchants with broken endpoints combined with synchronous per-delivery retries can saturate the 2000 concurrency budget, since each stuck HTTP call holds a slot for the full timeout window
bottlenecks.symptom: Receipt emails and push notifications lag by minutes to hours even though SMTP and APNs are healthy; Kafka consumer lag on payments.events climbs; on-call sees per-merchant delivery duration p99 pinned at the timeout ceiling and queue depth monotonically increasing
bottlenecks.mitigation: Isolate webhook delivery into a separate consumer group from email/push so one slow sink can't starve others; enforce a hard 10s HTTP timeout per webhook call; per-merchant bulkhead (max 10 concurrent in-flight deliveries per merchant_id) using a semaphore or token bucket; exponential backoff retries moved to a delayed-retry topic (not held in memory); circuit-break endpoints with >50% failure rate over 5min and auto-disable with merchant alert
bottlenecks.detection: Metric notif_webhook_duration_seconds histogram with alert on p99 >8s; notif_consumer_lag_seconds alert >60s on payments.events; per-merchant notif_webhook_failure_rate with alert >20% over 5min; notif_inflight_deliveries gauge vs. concurrency budget alert >70%

bottlenecks.title: Duplicate notifications from at-least-once Kafka delivery
bottlenecks.trigger: Orchestrator produces ChargeCaptured to Kafka fire-and-forget; consumer crash/rebalance between delivery and offset commit causes redelivery. At 1M charges/day with even 0.1% redelivery rate = ~1000 duplicate emails/webhooks/day; merchants integrating naively on webhook receipt may double-process orders
bottlenecks.symptom: Customer receives two identical receipt emails; merchant fulfillment system ships the order twice; support tickets about duplicate confirmations; merchant webhook endpoints log duplicate event IDs
bottlenecks.mitigation: Include a stable event_id (e.g., f"evt_{charge_id}_captured") in every Kafka message so downstream sinks can dedupe; for email/push, maintain a short-TTL Redis SETNX on event_id before dispatch (24h TTL); document to merchants that webhooks are at-least-once and they must dedupe on event_id; commit Kafka offsets only after successful dispatch acknowledgement
bottlenecks.detection: Metric notif_duplicate_event_id_suppressed_total with alert on sudden spikes; sample-based audit comparing count of charge.captured events in Kafka to count of distinct event_ids delivered — alert on >0.5% divergence; consumer rebalance rate metric with alert on >1/hour

bottlenecks.title: SMTP provider rate limits cause email backlog during traffic spikes
bottlenecks.trigger: 3x peak traffic (105 QPS of charge.captured events) fans out to receipt emails; most SMTP providers (SES, SendGrid) enforce per-second send quotas (e.g., SES default 14/sec, higher tiers 200–1000/sec). Peak burst can exceed quota during checkout rush (Black Friday, flash sales) even though daily average (12 QPS) is well within limits
bottlenecks.symptom: SMTP 454 Throttled responses spike; receipt email delivery lag grows from seconds to tens of minutes; customers complain they never got a receipt while their charge clearly succeeded; downstream retry logic amplifies load against the already-throttled provider
bottlenecks.mitigation: Token-bucket rate limiter in the email worker sized to 80% of provider quota with burst capacity; buffer overflow into a delayed-dispatch Kafka topic with staggered retry; pre-warm provider sending reputation and request quota increases ahead of known peak events; fallback to a secondary SMTP provider when primary returns throttling errors
bottlenecks.detection: Metric notif_smtp_throttle_rate with alert >0.1%; notif_email_dispatch_lag_seconds p95 alert >60s; daily email send volume dashboard vs. provider quota with alert at >70% utilization; SMTP provider API quota remaining metric polled every minute

prebuild.explanation: ## Why a Notification Service sits behind Kafka here For a payment system charging cards via Stripe, the charge pipeline is already doing expensive work on the critical path: a 200–800ms PSP call, a double-entry ledger transaction, a wallet update. Once the money has moved, you still owe the customer a receipt email, the merchant a webhook, and possibly a mobile push. These deliveries are **slow and unreliable** — SMTP providers throttle, merchant webhook endpoints time out, APNs occasionally rejects tokens. If the orchestrator did them inline, every flaky webhook would stretch checkout latency or, worse, roll back a perfectly good charge. The Notification Service exists so the orchestrator can fire-and-forget a Kafka event the moment the ledger commits, and let a separate worker pool handle the messy delivery problem on its own clock. ## What breaks without it Picture the orchestrator calling a merchant's webhook synchronously. The merchant's endpoint is returning 30s timeouts because their server is down. Now every charge for that merchant stalls for 30s, the orchestrator's concurrency budget (500 slots) fills up within seconds, and *other merchants' charges* start failing with 503s. One broken customer takes down checkout globally — while the ledger and PSP are perfectly healthy. ## The number At 1M charges/day with ~3 notifications each (email + push + webhook), that's **3M deliveries/day ≈ 35/sec average, ~105/sec at 3x peak**. With webhook p95 latencies routinely in seconds, 105 QPS × 5s average hold time = ~525 in-flight deliveries — exactly what the 2000-concurrency async worker pool is sized for, and exactly what you do *not* want blocking the 500-slot orchestrator. ## Trade-off Notifications become eventually-consistent (seconds to minutes of lag during incidents) in exchange for never letting a broken downstream sink stall a real payment.

operations.title: Charge (idempotent)
operations.name: Charge (idempotent)
operations.description: POST /v1/charges — first-time request. Idempotency claimed, PSP charged, ledger written, wallet credited, notification emitted.

steps.title: Client POSTs a charge with a fresh idempotency key
steps.action: Checkout page collects the card via Stripe Elements (tokenized client-side) and POSTs the charge with a UUIDv4 idempotency key.
steps.codeOrCommand:
POST /v1/charges HTTP/1.1
Host: payments.example.com
Authorization: Bearer mk_live_...
Idempotency-Key: 7f2c9e4b-a1d8-4a6f-9c2d-11b3e5a7d9f0
Content-Type: application/json { "amount_minor": 4999, "currency": "USD", "payment_method_token": "tok_visa_4242", "description": "Annual subscription"
}
steps.note: The client MUST reuse this same idempotency key on retry. Generating a new one per attempt defeats deduplication.

steps.title: LB terminates TLS and forwards to an API replica
steps.action: Least-connections routing across healthy API replicas. Public TLS terminated here; mTLS re-originated inward.
steps.codeOrCommand:
upstream = pool.pick(algo="least_connections", healthy_only=True)
forward(req → upstream, mtls=true)

steps.title: API validates request and claims idempotency key
steps.action: The API validates amount_minor is a positive integer, currency is ISO 4217, and the payment method token belongs to this merchant. Then it tries to claim the idempotency key in Redis with SET NX.
steps.codeOrCommand:
# 1. validate
assert isinstance(body.amount_minor, int) and body.amount_minor > 0
assert body.currency in ISO_4217
assert auth.merchant_owns(body.payment_method_token) # 2. claim idempotency key atomically
key = f"idem:{merchant_id}:{headers['Idempotency-Key']}"
claimed = redis.set(key, '{"status":"in_flight"}', nx=True, ex=86400)

steps.title: Redis claims the key (new request)
steps.action: SETNX succeeds because this is the first time we've seen this (merchant, key) pair in the last 24h. The key now holds an in-flight marker.
steps.codeOrCommand:
SET idem:mk_acct_42:7f2c9e4b-a1d8-4a6f-9c2d-11b3e5a7d9f0 '{"status":"in_flight"}' NX EX 86400
# returns OK (first writer wins)

steps.title: Orchestrator starts the saga
steps.action: API hands the request to the orchestrator, which allocates a charge_id and inserts a pending charge row before any external call. This row is our durable saga state.
steps.codeOrCommand:
charge_id = f"ch_{ulid.new}"
# saga step 1: persist intent BEFORE calling PSP
ledger.execute(""" INSERT INTO charges (id, merchant_id, idempotency_key, amount_minor, currency, status, created_at) VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, %s, 'pending', now)
""", (charge_id, merchant_id, idem_key, 4999, 'USD'))

steps.title: Ledger persists the pending charge row
steps.action: Single-row INSERT into charges under a short transaction. The UNIQUE (merchant_id, idempotency_key) constraint is a second line of defence against duplicates if Redis ever fails.

steps.title: Orchestrator calls the PSP (Stripe)
steps.action: The orchestrator calls Stripe with OUR charge_id as the Stripe Idempotency-Key. This is critical: if our process crashes between the HTTP send and receiving the response, a retry will find the same Stripe charge instead of creating a new one.
steps.codeOrCommand:
POST https://api.stripe.com/v1/charges
Authorization: Bearer sk_live_abcdef...
Idempotency-Key: ch_01HWX9ABC... # our charge_id amount=4999&currency=usd&source=tok_visa_4242 # Stripe responds (typical p50 ~200ms, p95 ~500ms)
{ "id": "ch_3OaStripeGeneratedId", "status": "succeeded", "amount": 4999, "currency": "usd", "paid": true
}
steps.note: External network hop — by far the longest segment of the flow. Timeout is 30s with 10s soft-retry using the same Idempotency-Key.

steps.title: Orchestrator writes double-entry in one transaction
steps.action: One SQL transaction flips the charge to captured AND writes the matched debit/credit pair. Either all three rows commit or none do — this is the atomicity guarantee that makes the ledger audit-provable.
steps.codeOrCommand:
BEGIN; UPDATE charges
SET status = 'captured', psp_charge_id = 'ch_3OaStripeGeneratedId'
WHERE id = 'ch_01HWX9ABC...'; -- Debit the customer (card) liability account
INSERT INTO ledger_entries (charge_id, account_id, direction, amount_minor, currency, posted_at)
VALUES ('ch_01HWX9ABC...', 'customer_card:tok_visa_4242', 'D', 4999, 'USD', now); -- Credit the merchant's available balance
INSERT INTO ledger_entries (charge_id, account_id, direction, amount_minor, currency, posted_at)
VALUES ('ch_01HWX9ABC...', 'merchant_balance:mk_acct_42', 'C', 4999, 'USD', now); COMMIT;

steps.title: Wallet updates the merchant balance view
steps.action: The materialized merchant balance is updated in the same transaction via a trigger (or a second statement before COMMIT). For clarity we show it as a separate step, but in practice it's part of the ledger transaction.
steps.codeOrCommand:
-- Inside the same ledger transaction
UPDATE account_balances
SET available_minor = available_minor + 4999
WHERE account_id = 'merchant_balance:mk_acct_42' AND currency = 'USD';

steps.title: Orchestrator emits ChargeCaptured event (fire-and-forget)
steps.action: A Kafka event triggers receipt email, merchant webhook, and push notification. Dispatched in parallel with preparing the API response — it does NOT delay the user.
steps.codeOrCommand:
kafka.produce( topic="payments.events", key="ch_01HWX9ABC...", value={ "type": "charge.captured", "charge_id": "ch_01HWX9ABC...", "merchant_id": "mk_acct_42", "amount_minor": 4999, "currency": "USD", "captured_at": "2026-04-24T14:02:18Z" }
)

steps.title: API overwrites idempotency key with final response
steps.action: Replace the in-flight marker with the full JSON response body. A retry within 24h gets byte-identical JSON back with no side effects.
steps.codeOrCommand:
redis.set( f"idem:{merchant_id}:{idem_key}", json.dumps({ "status": "done", "http_status": 201, "body": { "charge_id": "ch_01HWX9ABC...", "status": "captured", "amount_minor": 4999, "currency": "USD", "psp_charge_id": "ch_3OaStripeGeneratedId" } }), ex=86400
)

steps.title: API returns 201 Created
steps.action: The API builds the response from the orchestrator result and returns it to the LB.
steps.codeOrCommand:
return Response( status=201, headers={"Idempotency-Key": idem_key}, body={ "charge_id": "ch_01HWX9ABC...", "status": "captured", "amount_minor": 4999, "currency": "USD", "psp_charge_id": "ch_3OaStripeGeneratedId" }
)

steps.title: LB relays the response
steps.action: Return path through the load balancer; no routing decision needed.

steps.title: Client sees the captured charge
steps.action: Checkout page shows success. End-to-end latency is dominated by the PSP call (200–500ms); everything else adds up to ~20ms.

operations.title: Charge retry (idempotency key seen — cached replay)
operations.name: Charge retry (idempotency key seen — cached replay)
operations.description: Network flake causes the client to retry with the same idempotency key. Redis returns the cached response; no PSP call, no ledger write.

steps.title: Client retries with the SAME idempotency key
steps.action: The previous request's response timed out on the client side. The client retries — crucially, reusing the same Idempotency-Key.
steps.codeOrCommand:
POST /v1/charges HTTP/1.1
Idempotency-Key: 7f2c9e4b-a1d8-4a6f-9c2d-11b3e5a7d9f0 # SAME as before { "amount_minor": 4999, "currency": "USD",... }

steps.title: LB forwards — may land on a different replica
steps.action: This retry might land on a totally different API replica. That's fine — the idempotency state is external (Redis), not in-process.

steps.title: API checks idempotency store BEFORE validating or dispatching
steps.action: The first thing the API does on any mutating call is a Redis GET on the idempotency key. If it's present with status=done, replay the cached response.

steps.title: Redis returns the cached response
steps.action: The key was written on the original request's success path. It holds the full response body — no need to hit the PSP or the ledger again.
steps.codeOrCommand:
GET idem:mk_acct_42:7f2c9e4b-a1d8-4a6f-9c2d-11b3e5a7d9f0
# returns cached JSON from the original success
steps.decision: idempotency key seen — return cached result

steps.title: API replays cached 201 — no PSP call, no ledger write
steps.action: The API returns the byte-identical response the client would have received originally. Critically, the PSP was NOT called a second time and the ledger is unchanged.
steps.codeOrCommand:
return Response( status=201, body={ "charge_id": "ch_01HWX9ABC...", "status": "captured", "amount_minor": 4999, "currency": "USD", "psp_charge_id": "ch_3OaStripeGeneratedId" }
)
steps.note: This is where double-bills are prevented. Without this path, the retry would charge the card again — a very expensive bug in production.

steps.title: Client receives the same success it should have seen the first time
steps.action: The retry is indistinguishable from a successful original request. Total latency ~5–10ms because the hot path is entirely Redis.

operations.title: Refund
operations.name: Refund
operations.description: POST /v1/refunds — orchestrator calls PSP.refund, writes compensating ledger entries, debits the merchant balance.

steps.title: Merchant dashboard POSTs a refund
steps.action: Merchant admin clicks Refund on a captured charge. Dashboard POSTs with its own idempotency key.
steps.codeOrCommand:
